title: A Federal Judge Just Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. The Legal War Is Far From Over.
excerpt: Judge Leo Sorokin ruled the fee was an unlawful tax Congress never authorised. The decision directly benefits Indian workers who hold three-quarters of all H-1B approvals — but conflicting rulings in other courts guarantee a Supreme Court showdown.
body:
A federal judge in Boston struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas on Monday, ruling that the president exceeded his authority and imposed what amounts to an unlawful tax that Congress never authorised. The decision is the most significant legal blow yet to the controversial policy that has disrupted hiring plans across Silicon Valley and panicked hundreds of thousands of Indian tech workers.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin sided with 20 Democratic state attorneys general who argued that the fee had devastated their ability to recruit skilled workers for hospitals, schools, and universities. The ruling directly contradicts an earlier decision by a judge in Washington, D.C. who upheld the fee, setting up a potential Supreme Court battle that could define the limits of presidential authority over immigration policy.

## The Fee That Froze an Industry

The numbers tell the story of how effective the fee was at its stated purpose of discouraging foreign hiring. Before the fee was announced last September, H-1B visa applications typically cost employers between $2,000 and $5,000. The $100,000 surcharge made new petitions prohibitively expensive for all but the largest companies.

As of February 2025, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee. The programme that normally processes 85,000 new visa petitions annually had effectively ground to a halt for new applicants.

For the Indian diaspora, the impact was seismic. Nearly three-quarters of all H-1B visa approvals go to workers from India. The fee hit hardest in technology, healthcare, and education — sectors where Indian professionals are concentrated and where the visa is often the only pathway to legal employment.

## What the Judge Actually Said

Sorokin's 47-page ruling rejected the administration's argument that the fee was a lawful monetary penalty the president could impose under federal immigration law. The law gives the president power to restrict entry of foreign nationals when he deems it "detrimental to the interests of the United States." The administration argued this power extended to charging fees.

The judge disagreed, drawing on the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs under an emergency powers law. Just as the president lacked authority to levy tariffs without Congressional approval, Sorokin concluded, he lacked authority to impose what was effectively a tax on visa petitions.

"The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress," Sorokin wrote. "There are no statutory powers authorising Defendants to implement a $100,000 tax on H-1B petitions."

The ruling also invoked the Administrative Procedure Act, finding that the fee was imposed without the proper notice-and-comment process that federal regulations require.

## The Legal Mess Ahead

The ruling does not immediately resolve the situation for affected workers. A separate challenge by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C. resulted in Judge Beryl Howell siding with the administration in December, finding the fee lawful. That ruling is on appeal but left the fee in effect.

A third lawsuit, filed in San Francisco by religious groups and labour organisations, remains pending. The three cases are in different appellate court circuits, raising the possibility of contradictory rulings that would force the Supreme Court to intervene.

The White House signalled it would fight the decision. Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the administration was "confident" Sorokin's order would be reversed on appeal. "President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests," she said.

## What NRIs and Indian IT Companies Should Do Now

For Indian tech workers currently on H-1B visas, the immediate impact is limited. The $100,000 fee applies only to new petitions, not renewals. Workers already holding valid H-1B status are not affected.

For those awaiting new petitions, the ruling creates uncertainty rather than resolution. The fee remains technically in effect in jurisdictions covered by the D.C. ruling, and the administration is expected to appeal Sorokin's decision within weeks. Immigration attorneys recommend that employers planning new H-1B filings consult legal counsel on which court's ruling applies to their specific situation.

Indian IT outsourcing companies — Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL — which collectively sponsor thousands of H-1B visas annually, stand to benefit most if the fee is permanently struck down. Their stock prices, already battered by the broader technology selloff, could see relief if the Supreme Court ultimately sides with the challengers.

For the broader diaspora, the ruling underscores how deeply the H-1B programme is woven into the fabric of Indian-American life. It is the visa that brought engineers to Sunnyvale, doctors to rural hospitals, professors to research universities, and teachers to underfunded school districts. The fight over its future is, at its core, a fight over whether that pipeline remains open.

The fee is currently scheduled to expire in September 2026. Whether it survives that long — or whether the courts end it sooner — will depend on how quickly the appeals play out. For now, one federal judge has drawn a line: the president can restrict immigration, but he cannot tax it without Congress.
